record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses superposition as a proposed explanation for polysemanticity, but its experiments measure neuron-example clusters and an intentionally added SAE loss; they do not test the superposition or capacity claims in the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior superposition results and reports its own neuron-embedding and SAE-loss experiments. Those results concern polysemanticity proxies and the effects of the proposed training loss, not whether sparse features are superposed because of capacity pressure. Cited results from other work are not recorded. Values used to choose settings, such as the clustering threshold and activation cutoff, are not outcomes.
record.test_reason: The paper presents a method (neuron embeddings, plus an SAE loss built from them). It cites superposition only as the favoured explanation for polysemanticity. Its GPT2-small results are illustrative clusterings and comparisons of its own embedding against pre-MLP embeddings. Its MNIST results compare an SAE trained with its added loss against a standard SAE. None of these measure feature superposition, capacity pressure, distribution of features across neurons, or properties of SAE features as model units.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors also flag as a significant limitation that the method ignores features emerging only across several neurons.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce the original toy-model superposition method; it introduces neuron embeddings and an SAE training loss.

fits_no_version.finding: Neuron-embedding clustering splits example GPT2-small neurons into several distinct behaviours, e.g. six clusters, or a rare secondary behaviour at about 1:50.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual LLM neurons show multiple distinct, sometimes rare, behaviours that are recoverable by clustering weight-projected inputs.

fits_no_version.finding: Neuron embeddings give tighter, better-separated clusters than raw pre-MLP embeddings across GPT2-small neurons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weighting inputs by neuron input weights improves separation of a neuron's example behaviours.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding an NE loss to an MNIST SAE raises MSE, L0 and accuracy loss, and lowers embedding distances and dead neurons (23.8% to 3.7%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Penalising embedding dispersion in SAE training trades reconstruction and sparsity for proxy monosemanticity and fewer dead latents.

record.peer_reviewed: PMLR 235, 2024 (stated in the paper text); metadata also identifies arXiv.org
record.problems: The language-model clustering results are for GPT2-small and include illustrative neuron examples; the paper notes that it uses only the highest-activation token's pre-MLP embedding. The SAE-loss experiment is a proof of concept on a small MNIST toy model, and the authors state that transfer to larger models is unclear. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the tabulated results.

untested.parts: All: no toy-model study of features versus dimensions, sparsity transition or geometry.
All: the cause of polysemanticity is not investigated.
All: no alternative cause of polysemanticity is tested.
All: shows illustrative multi-behaviour GPT2-small neurons but does not measure feature distribution across neurons or recover LLM features with an SAE.
All: the SAE work is on an MNIST MLP and evaluates a training loss, not whether features are complete, stable or canonical.

record.verdict_notes: This is a method paper. Superposition is cited only in related work (Elhage 2022b; Gurnee 2023) and mentioned in passing in the conclusion. All GPT2-small evidence beyond Table 1 is illustrative single-neuron case studies. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

versions.untested_parts: Whether sparse features outnumber dimensions, overlap as nearly orthogonal directions, or show sparsity-dependent transitions and regular geometry.
Whether limited capacity causes polysemanticity, or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions while others share.
Whether polysemanticity arises for reasons other than capacity pressure, and whether it is or is not evidence of superposition.
Whether LLM features are distributed across many neurons or whether SAEs recover sparse features from LLMs.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, canonical units of a model's representation.
Whether superposed features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.
